query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating real‐time infrared feedback to dynamically modulate laser power during L‐PBF processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder will maintain a quasi‐isothermal melt pool, thereby reducing steep thermal gradients that cause compositional segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation, and ultimately improving mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock processed by conventional L‐PBF with fixed laser parameters.
generation.intervention: Implement dynamic thermal management via real‐time IR feedback-controlled laser power modulation during L‐PBF.
generation.conditions: L‐PBF additive manufacturing under standard processing conditions with rapid solidification, followed by mechanical testing under ambient to moderate service loads.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform microstructure with reduced microsegregation, lower residual stress distributions, and fewer processing defects.
generation.mechanism: By maintaining a quasi‐isothermal melt pool, the intervention minimizes steep thermal gradients that drive non-equilibrium solidification, which otherwise lead to compositional segregation, residual stress accumulation, and defect generation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventionally processed parts (with fixed laser settings), the dynamically controlled process is expected to yield parts with lower segregation and residual stresses, resulting in enhanced yield strength and fracture toughness.
generation.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi parts fabricated by conventional L‐PBF with fixed laser power settings.
generation.boundary: Valid for L‐PBF processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi under typical laser power and scan speed ranges; results are applicable under ambient to moderate operational temperatures typical of service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in mechanical properties and the extent of residual stress reduction are uncertain until systematically measured; reproducibility and process stability under dynamic control also require further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled experiment where identical cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder is processed in two sets: one using conventional fixed laser power L‐PBF, and the other using the proposed dynamic thermal management (IR feedback-controlled laser power modulation). Post‐processing, perform detailed microstructural analysis, residual stress measurement, and mechanical testing.
measurements: In situ melt pool temperature profiles
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for microsegregation
X-ray diffraction (XRD) or hole-drilling method for residual stress analysis
Tensile tests for yield strength and fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the parts produced with dynamic thermal management do not show statistically significant reductions in compositional segregation and residual stress, nor improvements in mechanical integrity (e.g., yield strength and fracture toughness), compared to the conventional processing, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Additive manufacturing (AM) is rapidly emerging as a pivotal technology for industrial part production due to its ability to create intricate shapes through computer-assisted layer-by-layer part construction. In metal AM, a broad, ever-expanding technology landscape has emerged with varying degrees of adoption in industry. While various AM technologies exist, liquid-mediated metal AM, notably Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), has garnered significant interest in industry and academia due to its potential to produce high-quality parts. L-PBF’s quality relies on understanding the interplay between process parameters, material properties, and solidification conditions. Traditional alloy design primarily targets specific manufacturing routes and often overlooks the unique demands of additive manufacturing (AM). In AM, designing alloys requires optimizing both chemistry and processing conditions simultaneously to minimize defects and enhance reliability. Conventional approaches first focus on achieving target properties and then on developing scalable processing methods. Manufacturing processes have a strong influence on the mechanical properties of HEAs. It has been determined that the CoCrFeNi part produced by the hot-rolling process has a better yield and ultimate strength compared to the casted parts [,,,]. Additive manufacturing processes, such as Laser-Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), can improve the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys due to their inherent unique processing characteristics. Specifically, the rapid solidification and repeated remelting associated with these techniques facilitate the formation of fine grains and numerous substructures with a high density of dislocations, thereby enhancing the yield strength compared to conventionally processed alloys. [] showed that the yield strength of the CoCrFeNi alloy produced by the powder bed fusion (PBF) process is twice, respectively, the treble of that alloy in as-cast condition, and Kuzminova [] showed in turn that the yield strength of alloys using L-PBF is twice than that of hot-rolled alloys. decision.trend: Early work on high‐entropy alloys has moved from alloy‐composition tuning in conventional bulk processes to adopting additive‐manufacturing routes such as selective laser melting and powder bed fusion. These studies have demonstrated that while rapid solidification can yield desirable phases and mechanical properties, the inherent steep thermal gradients result in compositional segregation, residual stresses, and defects. Incremental process parameter adjustments (e.g., laser power, scan speed) have been made but they leave unresolved the simultaneous control of microstructural uniformity and stress evolution.
decision.unsolved: A single processing intervention that can maintain a quasi–isothermal melt pool—thereby mitigating compositional segregation, reducing residual stresses, and limiting defect formation—remains unachieved.
decision.why: Following the observed trend that process‐parameter tuning alone cannot fully remedy rapid solidification issues, the most plausible next step is to integrate dynamic thermal management. By incorporating real‐time infrared feedback with laser power modulation during LPBF, the melt pool temperature can be controlled to approach isothermal conditions. This intervention directly addresses the root causes (high thermal gradients) that drive segregation, residual stresses, and defects in cobalt–free AlCrFeNiSi, promising improved mechanical integrity under service conditions.
